3.3.m:
Sūta said: / Thus addressed by her own lord, that queen of auspicious marks,
overcome with supreme astonishment, worshipped him with joy. / That king too, having enjoyed with her desired pleasures as he wished, / went at the end of the seven births to that supreme abode of Śambhu. / Whoever hears or even proclaims this most wondrous māhātmya of the worship of Śiva, / he shall go to the supreme abode. / Thus ends the fourth chapter, named 'The Description of the Māhātmya of the Fourteenth Day', in the Brahmottarakhaṇḍa, in the third [part of] the venerable Skandapurāṇa, a collection of eighty-one thousand [verses].
Sūta said:

3.3.s: śivo guruḥ śivo devaḥ śivo baṃdhuḥ śarīriṇām ..
3.3.d: शिवो गुरुः शिवो देवः शिवो बंधुः शरीरिणाम् ..
3.3.m: Śiva is the guru, Śiva is the god, Śiva is the kinsman of embodied beings.
Śiva is the Self, Śiva is the individual soul; there is nothing other than Śiva.
Whatever is given, whispered in prayer, offered into the fire, or performed with Śiva as the aim,
is declared to yield boundless fruit; this is determined by all sacred traditions.

3.3.s: bhaktyā niveditaṃ śaṃbhoḥ patraṃ puṣpaṃ phalaṃ jalam ..
3.3.d: भक्त्या निवेदितं शंभोः पत्रं पुष्पं फलं जलम् ..
3.3.m: A leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water offered with devotion to Śambhu,
even if exceedingly small, leads to endless reward.
Leaving aside all duties determined by all sacred traditions,
whoever worships Śiva alone is freed from all bondage.

3.3.s: yā prītirātmanaḥ putre yā kalatre dhanepi sā ..
3.3.d: या प्रीतिरात्मनः पुत्रे या कलत्रे धनेपि सा ..
3.3.m: Whatever affection one has for one's son, one's wife, or even for wealth,
if directed towards the worship of Śiva, what wonder is there that it saves?
Therefore, some great-souled persons abandon all worldly pleasures,
and even their own body, though hard to abandon, for the sake of worshipping Śiva.

3.3.s: sā jihvā yā śivaṃ stauti tanmano dhyāyate śivam ..
3.3.d: सा जिह्वा या शिवं स्तौति तन्मनो ध्यायते शिवम् ..
3.3.m: That is a tongue which praises Śiva; that is a mind which meditates on Śiva;

3.3.m: those are ears eager for his stories; those are hands that worship him;

3.3.s: te netre paśyataḥ pūjāṃ tacchiraḥ praṇataṃ śive ..

3.3.m: those are eyes that behold his worship; that is a head bowed down to Śiva;

3.3.s: tau pādau yau śivakṣetraṃ bhaktyā paryaṭataḥ sadā .. 8 ..
3.3.d: तौ पादौ यौ शिवक्षेत्रं भक्त्या पर्यटतः सदा .. 8 ..
3.3.m: those are feet that constantly wander through a sacred field of Śiva with devotion.
He whose senses are all engaged in deeds for Śiva,

3.3.s: sa nistarati saṃsāraṃ bhuktiṃ muktiṃ ca viṃdati .. 9 ..
3.3.d: स निस्तरति संसारं भुक्तिं मुक्तिं च विंदति .. 9 ..
3.3.m: crosses over worldly existence and attains enjoyment and liberation.
A mortal endowed with devotion to Śiva, even a cāṇḍāla or a pulkasa,

3.3.s: nārī naro vā ṣaṃḍho vā sadyo mucyeta saṃsṛteḥ .. 3.3.5.10 ..
3.3.m: a woman, a man, or a eunuch, is instantly freed from transmigratory existence.

3.3.m: What is the use of noble birth? What of traditional observances? What of good character or virtue?
One who possesses even a fraction of devotion to Śambhu is worthy of homage by all embodied beings.
In Ujjayinī there was a king named Candrasena,
born in human form like a second Indra.
To Mahākāla, the supreme lord residing in that city,
that Candrasena, the best of kings, rendered worship with devotion.
That king had a friend, the foremost attendant of Śiva,
named Maṇibhadra, who had conquered misfortune and was revered by all the worlds.
Once, pleased with that ruler of the earth, the follower of Śaṃkara,
the noble-minded Maṇibhadra gave him a divine wish-granting jewel.
That jewel, blazing like the Kaustubha and resembling the sun,

3.3.s: dṛṣṭaḥ śruto vā dhyāto vā nṛṇāṃ yacchati ciṃtitam .. 16 ..
3.3.d: दृष्टः श्रुतो वा ध्यातो वा नृणां यच्छति चिंतितम् .. 16 ..
3.3.m: granted whatever was wished for to people when seen, heard of, or meditated upon.
Touched by even a ray of its brilliance, bronze, copper, iron, tin,
stone, or anything else, instantly turned to gold.

3.3.s: sa taṃ cintāmaṇiṃ kaṃṭhe bibhradrājāsanaṃ gataḥ ..
3.3.d: स तं चिन्तामणिं कंठे बिभ्रद्राजासनं गतः ..
3.3.m: Wearing that wish-granting jewel on his neck and seated upon the royal throne,

3.3.s: rarāja rājā devānāṃ madhye bhānuriva svayam .. 18 ..
3.3.d: रराज राजा देवानां मध्ये भानुरिव स्वयम् .. 18 ..
3.3.m: the king shone like the sun itself in the midst of the gods.
Hearing of that best of kings whose neck always bore the wish-granting jewel,
all the kings, their greed inflamed, became agitated at heart.
Some asked for it out of friendship, while some, blinded by pride, out of arrogance.
The envious kings, unaware that the jewel was obtained from fate, (20)
when the request of all the kings had been rendered futile by him,
then the kings of all lands made preparations for battle. (21)
The Saurāṣṭras, Kaikayas, Śālvas, Kaliṅgas, Śakas, Madrakas,
Pāñcālas, Avantīs, Sauvīras, Māgadhas, Matsyas, and Sṛñjayas— (22)
these and other kings, accompanied by horses, chariots, and elephants,
made an effort with their might to conquer Candrasena in battle. (23)

3.3.s: te tu sarve susaṃrabdhāḥ kaṃpayaṃto vasundharām ..
3.3.d: ते तु सर्वे सुसंरब्धाः कंपयंतो वसुन्धराम् ..
3.3.m: All of them, fiercely agitated and making the earth tremble,
with numerous troops, blockaded the four gates of Ujjayinī. (24)
Seeing his city besieged by the arrogant kings,
Candrasena went to Mahākāla alone for refuge. (25)
Free from doubts, without food, and firm of resolve,
that king worshiped the lord of Gaurī day and night with undistracted mind. (26)
Meanwhile, a certain cowherd woman living in that city,
who had an only son, was without a husband, and was a long-time resident there, (27)

3.3.s: sā paṃcahāyanaṃ bālaṃ vahaṃtī gata bhartṛkā ..
3.3.d: सा पंचहायनं बालं वहंती गत भर्तृका ..
3.3.m: that widow, carrying her five-year-old child,
saw the great worship performed by the king for the husband of Girijā. (28)
Having witnessed all that wondrous magnificence of the worship of Śiva,
she bowed down and returned again to her own dwelling. (29)
Having watched all this in its entirety, that cowherd's son,
out of curiosity, performed a worship of Śiva that produces detachment. (30)

3.3.s: ānīya hṛdyaṃ pāṣāṇaṃ śūnye tu śibirottame ..
3.3.d: आनीय हृद्यं पाषाणं शून्ये तु शिबिरोत्तमे ..
3.3.m: Bringing an appealing stone into an empty, excellent tent
not far from his own dwelling, he set up a Śiva-liṅga. (31)

3.3.s: yāni kāni ca puṣpāṇi hastalabhyāni cātmanaḥ ..
3.3.d: यानि कानि च पुष्पाणि हस्तलभ्यानि चात्मनः ..
3.3.m: Whatever flowers were within reach of his hand,
bringing them and bathing that liṅga, he worshiped it with devotion. (32)
Fragrances, ornaments, garments, incense, lamps, unbroken rice, and the like—
having arranged these with makeshift, wonderful [substitutes], he also offered food. (33)
Having worshiped again and again with delightful leaves and flowers,

3.3.s: nṛtyaṃ ca vividhaṃ kṛtvā praṇanāma punaḥpunaḥ ..34..
3.3.d: नृत्यं च विविधं कृत्वा प्रणनाम पुनःपुनः ..34..
3.3.m: and having performed various dances, he bowed down repeatedly. (34)
While he was thus performing worship with a mind devoted solely to Śiva,

3.3.s: sā putraṃ praṇayādgopī bhojanāya samā hvayat..35..
3.3.d: सा पुत्रं प्रणयाद्गोपी भोजनाय समा ह्वयत्..35..
3.3.m: the cowherd woman, out of affection, called her son for a meal. (35)
Although called many times by his mother, his mind was attached to worship;

3.3.s: bālopi bhojanaṃ nacchattadā mātā svayaṃ yayau.. 36..
3.3.d: बालोपि भोजनं नच्छत्तदा माता स्वयं ययौ.. 36..
3.3.m: the boy did not want food, and then the mother came herself. (36)

3.3.s: taṃ vilokya śivasyāgre niṣaṇṇaṃ mī litekṣaṇam..
3.3.d: तं विलोक्य शिवस्याग्रे निषण्णं मी लितेक्षणम्..
3.3.m: Seeing him seated before Śiva with closed eyes,
she dragged him by taking his hand and struck him in anger. (37)
When her son did not come even though dragged or struck,

3.3.s: tāṃ pūjāṃ nāśayāmāsa kṣiptvā liṃgaṃ vidūrataḥ .. 38 ..
3.3.d: तां पूजां नाशयामास क्षिप्त्वा लिंगं विदूरतः .. 38 ..
3.3.m: she destroyed that worship, throwing the liṅga far away. (38)

3.3.s: hāheti rudamānaṃ taṃ nirbhartsya svasutaṃ tadā ..
3.3.d: हाहेति रुदमानं तं निर्भर्त्स्य स्वसुतं तदा ..
3.3.m: Reproaching her son who was crying out 'Alas, alas!',
the cowherd woman, filled with wrath, entered her own house again. (39)

3.3.s: mātrā vināśitāṃ pūjāṃ dṛṣṭvā devasya śūlinaḥ ..
3.3.d: मात्रा विनाशितां पूजां दृष्ट्वा देवस्य शूलिनः ..
3.3.m: Seeing the worship of the trident-bearing god destroyed by his mother,
that boy cried out, 'O God of gods!', and fell down. (40)
Having suddenly lost consciousness, flooded with a torrent of tears,
he regained consciousness after a moment and opened his eyes. (41)
Then, radiant with pillars of jewels, with golden doorways, door-leaves, and archways,
having a dais of priceless sapphires and flawless diamonds—that very tent had become a temple of Śiva. (42)
Charming with shining crystal palace floors, adorned with many colorful finials of refined gold,

3.3.s: ramyaṃ ca tacchivapuraṃ varapīṭhamadhye liṃgaṃ ca ratnasahitaṃ sa dadarśa bālaḥ .. 43 ..
3.3.d: रम्यं च तच्छिवपुरं वरपीठमध्ये लिंगं च रत्नसहितं स ददर्श बालः .. 43 ..
3.3.m: and delightful—in the middle of that splendid seat of Śiva's city, the boy beheld the liṅga together with jewels. (43)
Seeing this and rising up suddenly, his mind was frightened and astonished,
as if submerged out of satisfaction into an ocean of supreme bliss. (44)
Recognizing through its power the māhātmya of the worship of Śiva,
he bowed like a staff upon the ground for the pacification of his mother's sin: (45)
“O God, forgive the transgression of my mother, O lord of Umā!
Be gracious, O Śaṃkara, to the foolish woman who does not know you! (46)
If there is in me any religious merit whatsoever arisen from devotion to you,

3.3.s: tenāpi śiva me mātā tava kāruṇyamāpnuyāt .. 47 ..
3.3.d: तेनापि शिव मे माता तव कारुण्यमाप्नुयात् .. 47 ..
3.3.m: through that too, O Śiva, may my mother attain your compassion!” (47)

3.3.s: iti prasādya giriśaṃ bhūyobhūyaḥ praṇamya ca ..
3.3.d: इति प्रसाद्य गिरिशं भूयोभूयः प्रणम्य च ..
3.3.m: Having thus propitiated the mountain-dweller and bowed repeatedly,

3.3.s: sūrye cāstaṃ gate bālo nirjagāma śivālayāt .. 48 ..
3.3.d: सूर्ये चास्तं गते बालो निर्जगाम शिवालयात् .. 48 ..
3.3.m: when the sun had set, the boy went out from the temple of Śiva. (48)
Then he saw his own dwelling resembling the city of Purandara,
instantly turned into gold, ablaze with wonderful opulence. (49)
Entering inside the residence, rejoicing at the beginning of night, […]
filled with heaps of great gems, radiant with piles of gold. (50)
There he saw his mother, meditating, free from fear,
resting upon a white bed on a couch of precious jewels; (51)
her limbs shining with jewel ornaments, resplendent in celestial garments,
endowed with divine marks, like an apsaras in bodily form. (52)
With eyes wide with wonder, he quickly awakened her:

3.3.s: aṃba jāgṛhi bhadraṃ te paśyedaṃ mahadadbhutam.. 53 ..
3.3.d: अंब जागृहि भद्रं ते पश्येदं महदद्भुतम्.. 53 ..
3.3.m: "Mother, wake up! Blessings to you! Behold this great wonder!" (53)
Thus awakened by her noble-minded son,
smiling, radiant with a diadem, his mother then saw it. (54)
Rising in astonishment, she looked all around.
Looking upon herself as though unprecedented, and upon the boy as though unprecedented, (55)
and seeing her own home transformed, she was overwhelmed with joy.
Hearing from the son's mouth everything about the grace of Girijā's lord, (56)
she reported it to the king, who constantly worshipped Śiva.

3.3.s: sa rājā sahasāgatya samāpta niyamo niśi .. 57 ..
3.3.d: स राजा सहसागत्य समाप्त नियमो निशि .. 57 ..
3.3.m: The king, having completed his religious observances at night, arrived in haste; (57)
he saw the marvelous power of the cowherd's son, born of Śiva's satisfaction:
the golden temple of Śiva, and likewise the liṅga made of gems, (58)
and the cowherd woman's home, shining with excellent rubies.
Having seen everything, the king, together with his ministers and family priest, (59)
his composure arrested in wonder for a moment, filled with supreme bliss,
shed tears of love and embraced that boy. (60)
Thus, through the narration of Śiva's glory in this exceedingly wondrous manner,
and through the excitement of the citizens, that night passed like a single moment. (61)

3.3.s: atha prabhāte yuddhāya puraṃ saṃrudhya saṃsthitāḥ ..
3.3.d: अथ प्रभाते युद्धाय पुरं संरुध्य संस्थिताः ..
3.3.m: Then, at dawn, the kings who stood besieging the city for battle
heard the supreme wonder from the mouths of their spies. (62)
Immediately abandoning their enmity, greatly astonished,
the kings laid down their weapons and entered, welcomed by Candrasena. (63)

3.3.s: tāṃ praviśya purīṃ ramyāṃ mahākālaṃ praṇamya ca ..
3.3.d: तां प्रविश्य पुरीं रम्यां महाकालं प्रणम्य च ..
3.3.m: Entering that delightful city and bowing before Mahākāla,
all the kings went to the house of that cowherd woman. (64)
Going out to meet them, Candrasena honored them there;
seated on costly seats, they rejoiced with affection, filled with wonder. (65)
Beholding the temple of Śiva that had appeared for the grace of the cowherd's son,

3.3.s: liṃgaṃ ca vīkṣya sumahacchive cakruḥ parāṃ matim .. 66 ..
3.3.d: लिंगं च वीक्ष्य सुमहच्छिवे चक्रुः परां मतिम् .. 66 ..
3.3.m: and the immense liṅga, they directed their highest devotion to Śiva. (66)
Delighted, all those kings gave to that cowherd boy
garments, gold, gems, wealth such as cows and buffaloes, (67)
elephants, horses, golden chariots, parasols, vehicles, and attendants;
seeking the grace of Śiva, they gave many male and female servants. (68)
All the cowherds who lived in great numbers in all the regions—

3.3.s: teṣāṃ tameva rājānaṃ cakrire sarva pārthivāḥ ..69..
3.3.d: तेषां तमेव राजानं चक्रिरे सर्व पार्थिवाः ..69..
3.3.m: all the kings made him alone the king over them. (69)
Then, in the meantime, worshipped by all the thirty gods,
the radiant Hanūmān, lord of the monkeys, manifested himself. (70)
Merely upon his arrival, the kings, struck with reverence,
rose up and bowed down, their bodies bent low in devotion. (71)
Seated in their midst and worshipped, the lord of the monkeys,
embracing the cowherd's son, looked toward the kings and said: (72)

3.3.s: sarve śṛṇuta bhadraṃ vo rājāno ye ca dehinaḥ ..
3.3.d: सर्वे शृणुत भद्रं वो राजानो ये च देहिनः ..
3.3.m: "Listen, all of you—kings and whatever embodied beings are here! Blessings to you!
There is no other refuge for embodied beings than the worship of Śiva. (73)

3.3.s: eṣa gopasuto diṣṭyā pradoṣe maṃdavā sare ..
3.3.d: एष गोपसुतो दिष्ट्या प्रदोषे मंदवा सरे ..
3.3.m: By good fortune, on a Saturday at twilight (pradoṣa), this cowherd's son,
even without mantras, having worshipped Śiva, attained auspiciousness (śiva). (74)
This pradoṣa on a Saturday is rare to attain for all embodied beings;
even rarer is it when it falls in the dark fortnight. (75)
He is the most virtuous in the world, the enhancer of the cowherds' fame.
In his lineage, the eighth descendant will be of great renown, named Nanda;

3.3.s: prāpsyate tasya putratvaṃ kṛṣṇo nārā yaṇaḥ svayam .. 76 ..
3.3.d: प्राप्स्यते तस्य पुत्रत्वं कृष्णो नारा यणः स्वयम् .. 76 ..
3.3.m: Nārāyaṇa himself, Kṛṣṇa, will become his son. (76)
From this day forward, in this world, this son of the cowherd
shall attain lofty fame in the world by the name of Śrīkara. (77)"
Sūta said:
Having spoken thus, Añjanā's son [Hanūmān], having instructed that cowherd boy
in the righteous conduct of Śiva, vanished right there. (78)

3.3.s: te ca sarve mahīpālāḥ saṃhṛṣṭāḥ pratipūjitāḥ ..
3.3.d: ते च सर्वे महीपालाः संहृष्टाः प्रतिपूजिताः ..
3.3.m: And all those kings, delighted and mutually honored,
took leave of Candrasena and departed whence they had come.
Śrīkara too, of great splendor, instructed by Hanūmat,
worshiped Śambhu together with brahmins knowledgeable in dharma.
In the course of time, that Śrīkara and King Candrasena,

3.3.s: samārādhya śivaṃ bhaktyā prāpatuḥ paramaṃ padam .. 81 ..
3.3.d: समाराध्य शिवं भक्त्या प्रापतुः परमं पदम् .. 81 ..
3.3.m: having worshiped Śiva with devotion, attained the supreme abode.

3.3.s: idaṃ rahasyaṃ paramaṃ pavitraṃ yaśaskaraṃ puṇyamaharddhivardhanam ..
3.3.d: इदं रहस्यं परमं पवित्रं यशस्करं पुण्यमहर्द्धिवर्धनम् ..
3.3.m: This supreme secret, purifying, bringing renown, holy, and increasing great prosperity,
this narrative has been recounted, destroying heaps of sins and increasing devotion to the lotus feet of the Lord of Gaurī.

3.3.s: iti śrīskāṃde mahāpurāṇa ekāśītisāhasryāṃ saṃhitāyāṃ tṛtīye brahmottara khaṇḍe gopakumāracaritavarṇanaṃ nāma pañcamo'dhyāyaḥ .. 5 ..

3.3.m:
The seers said:
"The great and wondrous narrative that was spoken by you, O Sūta,
recounting the majesty of Śambhu, which removes all sins, is supreme.
We wish to hear that very same thing once more with attentive minds:
when the Lord Śambhu is worshiped at twilight by the great-souled,
what perfection does he bestow? Tell us this, O one of noble vows!
Even though heard repeatedly, O Sūta, our longing increases even more."
Sūta said:
"Well asked, O exceedingly wise ones, renowned throughout the world!
Therefore I shall declare the great fruit of worshiping Śiva.
The evening of the thirteenth lunar day is proclaimed as pradoṣa;
there Mahādeva must be worshiped by those desiring fruit, and no other deity.
Who indeed is capable of describing the majesty of pradoṣa worship,
wherein all the gods abide near the Lord of the Mountain?
At the time of pradoṣa, the Lord in Kailāsa, in his silver abode,
performs a dance, his rising virtues praised by the gods.
Therefore worship, recitation, oblations, stories of him, and praise of his virtues
must constantly be performed by mortals who desire the fruit of the four goals of life.
For mortals blinded by the darkness of poverty, fearful of worldly existence,
and sunken in the ocean of samsāra, this is a raft that shows the other shore.
For those afflicted by sorrow, grief, and fear, desiring the extinction of afflictions,
worshiping the Lord of Pārvatī at pradoṣa is the abode of all auspiciousness.
Even one of bad intellect, a base man, an unfortunate one, or a rogue,
having worshiped the Lord of the Gods at pradoṣa, is freed from calamities.
Even while being struck by enemies, or being bitten by serpents,
or being crushed by rocks, or fallen into the great ocean,
or smitten by the rod of death, or stricken by various diseases,
that mortal does not perish, because of worshiping the Lord of the Mountain at pradoṣa.
Poverty, death, sorrow, and a mountain-like burden of debt—
having dispelled them immediately, one is honored with prosperity through worshiping Śiva.
Here I shall relate an ancient, exceedingly holy legend,
hearing which all men attain the fulfillment of their aims.
In the realm of Vidarbha, there was a king named Satyaratha,
devoted to all righteousness, steadfast, virtuous, and true to his pledge.
While he ruled the earth according to dharma, O best of sages,
a long time passed in complete happiness for that great-minded one.
Then against that lord of the earth there arose Śālva kings,
enemies of arrogant might, led by Durmarṣaṇa.
Then on one occasion those Śālvas, having marshaled many soldiers,
arrived at the city of Vidarbha and besieged it, eager for victory.
Seeing that city being besieged, the ruler of Vidarbha
quickly marched out to fight, surrounded by a great army.
A battle took place between him and those Śālvas arrogant in their might,
like that between the lord of serpents in Pātāla and arrogant gandharvas.
Then that king of Vidarbha, having fought a most dreadful battle,
was slain at the head of the battle by the Śālvas, whose vast armies were destroyed.
When that heroic great chariot-warrior was slain along with his ministers,
the remaining broken soldiers fled from the battlefield.
Then, when the battle ceased and the enemy ministers shouted aloud,
while fighting was still occurring in the city and an uproar of noise arose,
a virtuous queen of that Satyaratha, the ruler of Vidarbha,
overcome with immense grief, departed somewhere with effort.
That king's pregnant wife, having departed with effort at night,
afflicted by sorrow, went toward the western direction.
Then, as morning broke, the virtuous woman, walking slowly along the road
after traversing a long path, saw a clear lake.
Having arrived there, the fair-hipped woman, scorched by intense heat,
took refuge beneath a shady tree blossoming on the shore of the lake.
There, by the power of destiny, in a secluded grove beneath the tree,
the virtuous woman gave birth to a son at an hour endowed with auspicious qualities.
Then that queen, stricken with severe thirst,
entered the lake, the fair-limbed woman, and was seized by a huge crocodile.
The prince, having just been born and now bereft of both father and mother,
wept loudly on the shore of the lake, feeble and tormented by hunger and thirst.
As that newborn prince was thus crying,
by good fortune a certain noble brahmin woman quickly arrived there.
Carrying her own one-year-old child,
she was destitute, bereft of a husband, and begging from house to house.
Having only one son, devoid of kinsmen, reduced to begging for alms,
that virtuous brahmin woman named Umā saw the prince.
Seeing that prince lying like a fallen orb of the sun,
helpless and crying, she thought at length:

You ought also to instruct a means to dispel the poverty / of this son of mine who lives only by food received as alms."
Śāṇḍilya said:
"That king of Vidarbha, the father of this boy,
was in his previous birth the lord of the Pāṇḍyas, an excellent king.
That king, knowing all duty, while protecting the entire earth,
once worshipped Śambhu at the time of dusk.
As he was worshipping the god, the lord of the three worlds, with devotion,
there arose everywhere in the city a great clamor.
Hearing that vehement sound, the king abandoned the worship of Śiva
and went out from the royal palace fearing a commotion in the city.
At that very moment, his minister of great might
captured an enemy vassal and came near the king.
Seeing the haughty enemy vassal brought by the minister,
the king, out of wrath, had his head cut off.
Having thus abandoned the worship of Śiva, that ruler of the earth,

His son also did likewise: at the time of dusk, Śiva
he did not worship; foolish and intoxicated with pride, he ate and went to sleep.
In another birth, that king became the ruler of Vidarbha.
Due to the interruption of the worship of Śiva, he was slain by enemies in the midst of enjoyments.
The one who was his son in that past existence has become his son in this birth;
he has fallen into poverty because of the transgression against the worship of Śiva.
His mother in a previous birth killed her co-wife through deceit.
Due to that great sin, she was slain by a crocodile in this existence.
This course of events regarding them has been related to you.
Mortals who leave Śiva unworshipped fall into poverty.
I speak the truth, I speak what is beneficial for the other world, I speak the essence, I speak the heart of the Upaniṣads: / having obtained this fierce and unsubstantial saṃsāra, a living being's only essence is service to the lotus-feet of Īśvara.
Having obtained this dreadful, essenceless cycle of rebirth, this is a creature's essence: service to the lotus feet of Īśvara.
Those fools who do not worship the Mountain-Dweller at the time of dusk, / and those others who do not bow even to Śiva when he is worshipped, / nor drink in his story with the cups of their ears—those men become poor in birth after birth.

3.3.m:
Fools who do not drink this discourse with the hollows of their ears—such men become poor in birth after birth.
Those who, at the time of dusk, with single-minded devotion perform the worship of the lotus-feet of the Supreme Lord,
they, even in this world, are constantly preeminent, endowed with ever-increasing wealth, grain, wives, sons, good fortune, and prosperity.
Having seated Gaurī, the mother of the three worlds, on a jewel-throne adorned with gold in the mansion on Mount Kailāsa, / when the Trident-Bearer desires to perform his dance, all the gods attend upon him at the time of dusk.
When the trident-bearer desires to perform his dance, all the gods attend upon him at the evening twilight.
The goddess of speech holds the lute; the hundred-sacrificer holds the flute; the lotus-born claps his hands to mark the beat; the divine Ramā accompanies with the practice of song;
Viṣṇu is skilled at playing the deep-sounding drum; standing all around, the gods serve that deity, the husband of Mṛḍānī, at the time of dusk.
The hosts of gandharvas, yakṣas, birds, serpents, siddhas, sādhyas, / vidyādharas, the foremost immortals, and apsarases,
and whatever other inhabitants of the three worlds there are, along with the hosts of spirits, stand at Hara's side when the time of dusk arrives.

Therefore, at dusk, Śiva alone is to be worshipped, and not others such as Hari and the Lotus-Born.
When that Great Lord is worshipped according to rule, all the lords of the gods are pleased.
This son of yours, in his previous birth, was an excellent brahmin.
he spent his life accepting gifts, not in good deeds such as sacrifices. (80)
Therefore, O noble brahmin lady, your son has fallen into poverty.
To remove that defect, let him take refuge in Śaṃkara. (81)

"One must not go forward from here; women are sporting ahead. / Wise men of pure heart avoid the proximity of women.
They are deceivers, proud with the intoxication of wealth and youth, / who bewilder people on sight, skilled in cajoling speech.
Therefore one should shun the presence of women and conversing with them, / especially a wise celibate student devoted to his own duty.
Therefore, I do not dare to go to the playground of these deer-eyed women." / Having spoken thus, the brahmin's son turned back and stood at a distance.
Then that prince, his mind filled with curiosity, / went entirely alone and fearless along the path of their amusement.
There, among the Gandharva maidens, one fair-faced maiden / seeing the prince approaching, reflected in her mind:
"Oh, who is this noble-limbed youth, handsome in every part of his body, / walking like an elephant in rut, an ocean of the nectar of beauty?
He has wide eyes that dart playfully, charming with a sweet smile, / endowed with the grace of love's god himself, bearing the marks of delicate limbs."

All of you go to that grove, gather a heap of flowers, / and return; meanwhile, I shall remain right here."
Thus commanded, the troop of female companions went to another grove; / and that Gandharva maiden remained, fixing her gaze upon the prince.
Beholding that slender-limbed maiden, endowed with fresh youth, / who by the abundance of her beauty surpassed even Tilottamā,
the prince, approaching with eyes wide in wonder, / experienced the agony of love's arrow by the stroke of fate.
That Gandharva maiden too, as the prince approached, / stood up quickly and offered him a seat of tender sprouts.
Approaching him as he sat after receiving hospitality, the slender-waisted maiden, / her senses agitated and her firmness broken by his beauty and virtues, asked:
"Who are you, lotus-petal-eyed one? From what country have you come here? / Whose son are you?" Asked thus with affection, he related everything:

let no breach in our mutual affection ever arise henceforward.'

You, a young maiden under a father's authority, transgressing your father's command—
how is it proper for you to act independently, like a foolish girl?'
Hearing his words, she of pure smiles said to him:
'So be it! I shall act in that very way; behold a wondrous thing!
Go to your abode, my beloved, but the day after tomorrow, early in the morning,
come right back here; we have business, and it is no lie.'
Having said this to that prince, she joined her companions;
the fair-limbed maiden departed, and the prince departed as well.
Having joyfully gone into the presence of the brahmin's son,
he related everything and went with him to his own abode.
And having delighted that virtuous brahmin woman again, the prince,
on the day after tomorrow, went to the forest together with that son of the brahmin.
Reaching the place indicated earlier by her, the prince
saw the king of the Gandharvas accompanied by his daughter.

Welcoming the two youths who had arrived, the lord of the Gandharvas
seated them on a delightful seat and spoke to the prince.
The Gandharva said:
'O prince, yesterday I went to Kailāsa;
there I saw the Lord Mahādeva together with Pārvatī.
Calling me, that Lord of gods, in the presence of all the dwellers of heaven,
the blessed Lord, an ocean of the nectar of compassion, said:
"There is a prince on earth named Dharmagupta,
destitute, fallen from his kingdom, his land seized by enemies.
Following the guru's instruction, that boy is ever devoted to my worship;
today all his ancestors have attained me through his power.
You too must lend him assistance, O best of Gandharvas;
then he will be established in his own kingdom, his enemies slain."
Commanded thus by Maheśa, I returned to my own palace,
and I was repeatedly beseeched in this manner by this daughter of mine.

3.3.m:
I took this daughter and came to this inner forest.
Therefore, I bestow this maiden, Aṃśumatī, upon you;
slaying your enemies, I shall establish you in your own kingdom by the command of Śiva.
Having enjoyed desires as you wish together with her in that city,
at the end of ten thousand years you will go to the abode of the Mountain-Dweller.
Even there, this daughter of mine will obtain you alone,
with this very divine body, in the presence of Śiva.'
Having spoken thus to the prince, the king of the Gandharvas
arranged the marriage of his daughter in that forest.
He gave him dowry: loads of exceedingly brilliant gems,
a crest-jewel resembling the moon, and radiant necklaces of pearls,
divine ornaments and garments, equipage made of gold,
ten thousand elephants, and a hundred thousand dark horses,
thousands of great golden chariots,
moreover, a divine chariot and a bow resembling Indra's rainbow,
thousands of divine weapons, and two quivers with inexhaustible arrows.

3.3.m:
Impenetrable golden armor, and a lance that crushes enemies,
five thousand servant-women to attend upon his daughter,
and various treasures did he give to him with a delighted heart.
A formidable gandharva army, equipped with all four divisions,
the king of gandharvas further gave to assist him.
Thus the prince attained supreme prosperity;
accompanied by his desired wife, he rejoiced in his good fortune.
Having celebrated his daughter's wedding as befitted the occasion,
the king of gandharvas mounted his vimāna and went to heaven.
Having entered into marriage, Dharmagupta, accompanied by the gandharva army,
returned to his own city and smote the host of enemies.
Having slain the invincible [foe] in battle with his lance and the gandharva army,
and having completely destroyed the enemy forces, he entered his own city.
Then, consecrated by ministers and foremost brahmins,
mounted upon a jeweled lion-throne, he ruled a kingdom free of adversaries.

3.3.m:
That brahmin woman who had formerly nourished him like her own son,
became his mother, and the brahmin boy his brother.
With the gandharva maiden as his wife, lord of the city of Vidarbha,
having worshiped the god Giriśa, Dharmagupta became king.
In the same way, others who thoroughly worship the husband of the Mountain's Daughter at dusk (pradoṣa)
attain their desired wishes, and at the end of the body, the supreme state.
Sūta said:
This holy, great observance—the worship of Śaṃkara at pradoṣa—
is the supreme means to achieve duty, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.
Whoever hears this sacred and most wondrous māhātmya,
or recites it attentively at the conclusion of Śiva's worship at pradoṣa,
shall not suffer poverty even in a hundred future births;
endowed with knowledge and sovereignty, at the end he goes to the city of Śiva.
Blessed indeed are those mortals who, having attained this most rare human body, perform the worship of the feet of the Supreme Lord!
They have conquered the three worlds through their merit; the dust of their lotus feet purifies the world.

3.3.m: Sūta said: / Thus addressed by the sage, that virtuous brahmin woman / bowed to him and then asked the procedure for worshiping Śiva. (1) / Śāṇḍilya said: / When one fasts on the thirteenth day of either fortnight, / three ghaṭīs before sunset one should take a ritual ablution. (2) / Wearing white garments, steadfast, restrained in speech, bound by vows, / having performed the prescribed twilight prayers and recitation, he should begin the worship of Śiva. (3) / Having smeared the ground before the god properly with fresh water, / and constructed a charming maṇḍala with clean cloths and other materials, the wise man, (4) / adorning it with canopies and the like, with fruits, flowers, and fresh sprouts, / drawing a variegated lotus endowed with the five colors, (5) / sitting there upon a steady, very auspicious seat, endowed with devotion, / having properly procured all the worship implements, being pure, (6) / the intelligent man should consecrate the seat with the mantra spoken in the scriptures. / Then, having performed purification of oneself and purification of the elements and the rest in proper order, (7) / having performed three breath-controls with the seed-syllables accompanied by the dot, / having deposited the letters of the alphabet according to rule, and meditating on that supreme deity, (8) / having completed the alphabet, and then meditating once again on supreme Śiva, / bowing to the guru on the left side, he should bow to Gaṇapati on the right. (9) / Having deposited Dharma and the others on the pair of shoulders and thighs, and on the navel and the two sides / Adharma and the others, and Ananta and the others, he should deposit the mantra upon the heart-seat. (10) / Beginning with the foundational power, following in order up to the nature of wisdom, / having deposited them in the stated order upon the lotus of the heart properly visualized, (11) / which is delightful and consists of the nine powers, he should meditate on the god, the lord of Umā: / resembling ten million moons, three-eyed, bearing the crescent moon upon his crest, (12) / with reddish-brown matted locks, radiant with a jewel-encrusted crest, / blue-necked, of noble form, adorned with a serpent-necklace, (13) / with hands granting boons and fearlessness, holding an axe, / wearing serpent-bracelets, upper armlets, armlets, and rings, (14) / clad in a tiger skin, seated upon a jeweled throne.

3.3.m: Having meditated [upon him], on his left side he should visualize the Daughter of the Mountain: (15) / lustrous like a blooming hibiscus flower, having the radiance of the rising sun, / resembling a flash of lightning, slender, delighting the mind and eyes, (16) / bearing the crescent moon on her crest, glossy, with dark curled hair, / charming with swarms of bees, adorned with dark forelocks, (17) / the graceful play of her round face illuminated by jeweled earrings, / her mirror-like cheek-halves marked with fresh saffron paste, (18) / her sprout-like red lower lip shining with a sweet smile, / conch-necked, auspicious, with lotus-bud breasts rising up, (19) / possessing four radiant arms with the noose, the goad, and gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting, / adorned with rings and bracelets glittering with many jewels, (20) / endowed with a golden girdle-string shining above three folds [of the waist], / wearing a red garland and red garments, anointed with divine sandalwood paste, (21) / her lotus feet bowed to by the crests of the wives of the guardians of the directions, / mounted on a jeweled throne, with the king of serpents as her ornament. (22) / Having thus meditated on Mahādeva and the goddess, the Daughter of the Mountain, / and having worshiped the god with perfumes and other offerings in the order of ritual deposition, (23) / he should offer [worship] with the five Brahmamantras in the prescribed places or in the heart, / and a separate handful of flowers upon the body, and thrice upon the heart with the primary mantra. (24) / Then, the practitioner himself becoming Śiva by means of the primary mantra, / he should then worship the god again in sequence on the external seat. (25) / Being composed, he should state the solemn resolve there at the beginning of the worship. / Having joined his hands in reverence, he should contemplate Śaṃkara in his heart: (26) / 'For the removal of debt, sin, misfortune, and poverty, / for the destruction of all sins, be gracious to me, O Śaṃkara! (27) / Tormented by the fire of sorrow and grief, afflicted by the fear of worldly existence, / distressed by many diseases, wretched—save me, O rider of the bull! (28) / Come, O lord of the gods of gods, O Mahādeva, bestower of fearlessness! / Receive, together with Pārvatī, your worship performed by me.' (29) / Having made this solemn resolve according to rule, he should perform the worship of the Absolute.

3.3.m: One should worship the Guru and Gaṇapati on the left and right; / one should worship the lord of the field in the northeast corner, and then Vāstoṣpati in proper order; / one should worship Vāgdevī there, and then worship Kātyāyanī. / [One should worship] righteousness, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereign power with vowels ending in 'namaḥ' / in the corners starting from the northeast, [as] the feet of the pedestal in succession. / With these two, the bindu and the visarga, one should worship unrighteousness and the others. / In the four directions in the forms of sattva, and in the center Ananta together with the Tāraka [mantra]; / one should install the three guṇas—sattva and the rest—in those forms upon the pedestal. / Above its covering, [one should place] Māyā along with Lakṣmī and Śiva. / At the end of that, furthermore, a lotus, the complete threefold maṇḍala, / covered with petals, filaments, and anthers, inscribed in order with the letters of the Tāraka. / Having thus worshipped the three lotuses, devoutly in the middle of the maṇḍala, / one should worship Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī in the cardinal directions beginning with the eastern division. / One should worship the nine Śaktis, beginning with Vāmā, accompanied by the nine vowels; / and one should worship [them] in the heart with the pedestal mantra preceded by the three seed-syllables. / Surrounded by the first limbs in circumambulation, and by the five forms and Śaktis, / and by the three Śakti forms, and by others endowed with the two treasures, / encircled by Ananta and the rest, by the Mothers, by the Bull and others, / by the supernatural powers beginning with aṇimā, and by Indra and the others along with their weapons; / the Bull, Kṣetrapāla, Caṇḍeśa, Durgā, Skanda, and Nandin, / Gaṇeśa, and the commander of the army, each characterized by their respective marks; / aṇimā, mahimā, garimā, and laghimā, / īśitva, vaśitva, prāpti, and prākāmya— / these are declared to be the eight sovereign powers, consisting purely of light; / previously with the five Brahmamantras, in order beginning with Hṛllekhā, / the worship with the limbs, Umā and others, and Indra and others, was declared by those sages. / One should worship Umā, Caṇḍeśvara, and the others starting from the north. / In this way, Sadāśiva, the embodiment of light, endowed with these surrounding deities,

3.3.m: the God accompanied by Umā, should be worshipped with the offerings. / Having bathed Mahādeva with waters from a well-established conch and with the five nectars, / composed in mind, with the Rudrasūktas, / one should arrange the offerings such as the seat with diverse mantras. / One should arrange a golden seat furnished with divine cloth. / With pure water, one should offer the arghya endowed with eightfold qualities, and the pādya; / with the same, one should offer the water for sipping, and the madhuparka rich in honey. / Having offered water for sipping again, one should perform the bath with mantras. / One should offer the sacred thread, clothing, and ornaments; / one should offer highly purified perfume consisting of eight ingredients. / And then the bilva, mandāra, kahlāra, lotus, / dhattūra, karṇikāra, hemp-flower, and jasmine, / kuśa, apāmārga, tulasī, mādhavī, campaka, and others, / bṛhatī, and oleander, as they are obtained—the practitioner / should present fragrant and diverse garlands; / incense produced from black aloe, and a spotless, auspicious lamp, / [and] an unguent mark. / Then an offering of milk-rice accompanied by ghee and side dishes, / accompanied by modakas and sweet cakes, mixed with sugar and jaggery, / anointed with honey, combined with curds, and provided with drinking water; / with that very oblation, one should sacrifice into the fire energized with mantras, / according to the rite prescribed in the Āgama, guided by the words of the guru. / Having offered food to Śambhu, [one should offer] once more excellent betel, / incense, a charming waving of lights, a parasol, and an excellent mirror, / having presented them duly with Vedic and Tantric mantras. / If one is unable oneself and destitute, one should worship according to one's means; / the Lord of Gaurī is pleased with merely a flower offered with devotion. / Then one should worship all who form his retinue, beginning with Gaṇeśa; / having praised him with various hymns, the wise one should bow down with the eight-limbed prostration. / Then, having circumambulated the Bull, Caṇḍeśvara, and the rest,

3.3.m: and having duly offered the worship, one should pray to the husband of Girijā: / 'Victory, O God, Lord of the universe! Victory, O eternal Śaṃkara! / Victory, O presiding Lord of all gods! Victory, O one worshipped by all gods! / Victory, O one beyond all qualities! Victory, O bestower of all boons! / Victory, O eternal one without support! Victory, O imperishable supporter of the universe! / Victory, O Lord known only through the universe! Victory, O one adorned with the king of serpents! / Victory, O husband of Gaurī, O Śambhu! Victory, O one with the crescent moon on your crest! / Victory, O one resembling ten million suns! Victory, O refuge of infinite virtues! / Victory, O Rudra, Virūpākṣa! Victory, O inconceivable, taintless one! / Victory, O Lord, ocean of compassion! Victory, O dispeller of the distress of devotees! / Victory, O Master who carries across the ocean of transmigration that is hard to cross! / Be pleased with me, O Mahādeva, who am distressed and grieving in transmigration; / having removed all fear of sin, protect me, O Parameśvara! / Sunk in great poverty, struck down by great sin, / ruined by great sorrow, afflicted by severe disease, / burdened by the weight of debt, tormented by my past actions, / afflicted by the planets—be gracious to me, O Śaṃkara!' / A poor man should thus pray at the end of worship to the husband of Girijā; / or a wealthy man, or a king, should pray to the divine Lord: / 'May long life, constant health, increase of treasury, and elevation of strength, / [and] perpetual joy be mine through your grace, O Śaṃkara! / May my enemies go to destruction; may my planets be propitious; / may robbers perish in the kingdom; may the people be free from calamity; / may famine, plague, and distress come to pacification upon the earth; / may there be abundance of all crops, and may all directions be full of happiness!' / In this manner one should worship the God, the husband of Girijā, at twilight; / afterwards, one should feed brahmins and satisfy them with gifts. / Bringing destruction to all sins, destroying all poverty, / the worship of Śiva that bestows all desired boons has been proclaimed by me. / The multitude of great mortal sins, as well as minor sins...

3.3.m: One should refrain from everything else rather than steal Śiva's property. / In the Purāṇas and in the Smṛtis, expiations are seen / for sins such as killing a brahmin, but not for those who steal Śiva's property. / What is the use of saying much on this matter? I state it in half a verse: / Worship of Śiva destroys even a hundred killings of a brahmin. / This worship of Śiva at twilight (pradoṣa) has been told to you by me, / the secret for all living beings; there is no doubt about this. / Let worship be performed in this manner even by these two boys; / from this, in just one year, you will attain supreme perfection." / Having heard these words of Śāṇḍilya, the brahmin woman, / together with those two boys, bowed down at the sage's feet. / The brahmin woman said: / "Today I have achieved my life's purpose merely by seeing you. / O venerable one, these two boys have gone to you alone for refuge. / O brahmin, this is my son, called Śucivrata; / this one is a prince, named Dharmagupta by me. / These two and I, O venerable one, are the servants of your feet; / rescue us who have fallen into this dreadful ocean of poverty." / Having thus comforted with words sweet as nectar the brahmin woman who had sought refuge, / the sage then instructed those two boys in the knowledge of the mantra for worshipping Śiva. / Then, instructed by the sage, the two boys and that brahmin woman, / having bowed to him and taken their leave, departed from the temple of Śiva. / From that time onward, those two boys, by the instruction of the excellent sage, / readily performed the worship of Pārvatī's lord at twilight. / As the brahmin boy and the prince were thus worshipping the god, / four months passed for them in utter happiness. / Once, without the prince, that son of the brahmin / went to bathe on the riverbank and wandered about in playful delight. / There, in an embankment wall split open by the torrent of a waterfall, / he saw a large, glittering treasure jar.

3.3.m: Seeing it, having approached quickly, overcome with joy and curiosity, / thinking it obtained by divine providence, he took it up on his head and went away. / Bringing it with haste and putting down the jar by force, / placing it inside the house, he spoke to his mother: / "Mother! Mother! Look at this favor of the lord of the mountain's daughter! / A treasure has been revealed in the form of a pot by the compassionate one!" / Then the virtuous woman, astonished, called the prince, / and, congratulating her own son while honoring the worship of Śiva, she said: / "Listen to my words, my two sons: divide this treasure jar / equally and take it, out of respect for my command." / Hearing these words of his mother, the brahmin boy was pleased; / the prince, confident in the worship of Śaṃkara, replied to her: / "Mother, it has arrived solely by the merit of your son; / I do not wish to take a divided store of wealth. / Let him enjoy by himself what was obtained from his own merit; / that same divine Lord will show mercy to me." / As they thus worshipped Śambhu once again with supreme delight, / a year passed for them in that very house. / Then one day, when the spring season arrived, the prince, / together with that brahmin, wandered in the midst of a forest. / Then, having gone far away somewhere in the forest, the brahmin boy and the prince / saw hundreds of Gandharva maidens playing. / Seeing all of them, charming in all their limbs and strolling delightfully, / the brahmin's son said to the prince from afar:

3.3.m: Who is the creator even of the creator, and the cause of the cause itself, / the supreme light among lights—that Śiva is our ultimate refuge.

3.3.m:
Sūta said: / Hearing this speech of his, Takṣaka, pleased in mind, / with devotion awakened towards Mahādeva, spoke to the prince.
Takṣaka said:
'I am well pleased; may good fortune be yours, O son of an excellent king!
Since, though a boy, you know the highest reality pertaining to Śiva, higher than the highest.
This world is full of jewels, and these women are lovely-eyed.
"All these are wishing-trees; the step-wells have waters of nectar-essence.
Here there is no terrible fear of death, nor the torment of old age and disease.
Sport here at your pleasure; enjoy the delights as befit you."
Thus addressed by the king of serpents, that prince,
noble in mind, replied with supreme affection, his hands joined in reverence:
"I have taken a wife at the proper time; my wife is faithful to her vows,
constantly devoted to the worship of Śiva; my parents have but an only son.
Believing me dead today, overwhelmed with great sorrow,
they will surely part with their lives, or else barely breathe by fate.
Therefore, I must by no means remain here for many days.

3.3.m:
You ought graciously to convey me back to that very world."
To the prince who spoke thus, having refreshed [him] with divine, excellent food born of celestial trees,
with excellent perfumes, garments, garlands, gems, and varied divine ornaments,
and having gratified [him] with various pleasures, the king of serpents said again:
"Whenever you remember [it], it shall be manifested before you by me!"
Moreover, to the prince Takṣaka gave a horse that went at will,
[moving] without hindrance through various continents, oceans, and worlds.
He gave jeweled ornaments, divine decorations, and garments;
and to carry them, the lord of serpents gave a rākṣasa.
And appointing a prince of serpents to assist him,
Takṣaka dismissed him with affection, saying, "Go!"
Thus taking the various riches, that Candrāṅgada,
mounting the horse that went at will, departed with the two of them.

he roved on the delightful bank, mounted on the divine steed.
Now at that time, the slender and virtuous Sīmantinī
came there to bathe, surrounded by her companions.
She saw the prince sporting on the riverbank,
accompanied by the rākṣasa in human form and by the son of the serpent,
strewn with divine jewels, wearing a crest of divine garlands,
his body diffusing a divine fragrance over ten yojanas.
Seeing him of extraordinary form, mounted on the divine horse,
she stood, her eyes fixed on him, as if stunned, crazed, or frightened.
And the prince, recalling that she had been seen before,
[saw that she was] stripped of throat ornaments, devoid of the auspicious necklace,
her hair unbraided, without bodily unguents,
the corners of her eyes free of black collyrium, thin-limbed, marred by grief.
Seeing [her], he dismounted from the horse, sat down on the riverbank,
and calling that woman of lovely hips, had her sit down and said this:
"Who are you? Whose wife, or whose virtuous daughter are you?

किमिदं तेंगने बाल्ये दुःसहं शोकलक्षणम् .. 3.3.8.120 ..
इति स्नेहेन संपृष्टा सा वधूरश्रुलोचना ..
लज्जिता स्वयमाख्यातुं तत्सखी सर्वमब्रवीत् .. 21 ..
इयं सीमंतिनी नाम्ना स्नुषा निषधभूपतेः ..
चंद्रांगदस्य महिषी तनया चित्रवर्मणः .. 22 ..
अस्याः पतिर्दैवयोगान्निमग्नोऽस्मिन्महाजले ..
तेनेयं प्राप्तवैधव्या बाला दुःखेन शोषिता .. 23 ..

.. सूत उवाच .. ..

ततः सीमंतिनी प्राह स्वयमेव नृपात्मजम् .. 27 ..
3.3.m:
Why, O fair woman, is this unbearable sign of grief in your youth?"
Thus asked with affection, that young woman, tears in her eyes,
was too bashful to speak herself; her companion told everything:
"This is Sīmantinī by name, daughter-in-law of the king of Niṣadha,
the queen of Candrāṅgada, daughter of Citravarman.
Her husband, by a stroke of fate, drowned in these vast waters;
thereby this young girl has fallen into widowhood and is wasted by sorrow.
In this way three years have passed in overwhelming grief.
Today, Monday having arrived, she came here to bathe.
Her father-in-law, a mighty king, has been deprived of his kingdom by enemies,
seized by force, bound, and remains in their power together with his wife.
Even so, this woman of auspicious conduct, on Monday,
worships Maheśvara together with Ambikā with supreme devotion and a pure mind."
Sūta said:
Having thus made everything known through the mouth of her friend, the woman of good vows,
Sīmantinī then spoke to the prince herself:

3.3.s:
kastvaṃ kaṃdarpasaṃkāśaḥ kāvimau tava pārśvagau ..

kimarthaṃ mama vṛttāṃtaṃ snehavāniva pṛcchasi ..

dṛṣṭapūrva ivābhāsi mayā ca svajano yathā ..
sarvaṃ kathaya tattvena satyasārā hi sādhavaḥ .. 3.3.8.130 ..
.. sūta uvāca ..
etāvaduktvā naradevaputrī sabāṣpakaṃṭhaṃ suciraṃ ruroda ..

śrutvā caṃdrāṃgadaḥ sarvaṃ priyāyāḥ śokakāraṇam ..

athāśvāsya priyāṃ tanvīṃ vividhairvākyanaipuṇaiḥ ..

3.3.d:
कस्त्वं कंदर्पसंकाशः काविमौ तव पार्श्वगौ ..
देवो नरेंद्रः सिद्धो वा गंधर्वो वाथ किन्नरः .. 28 ..
किमर्थं मम वृत्तांतं स्नेहवानिव पृच्छसि ..
किं मां वेत्सि महाबाहो दृष्टवान्किमु कुत्रचित् .. 29 ..
दृष्टपूर्व इवाभासि मया च स्वजनो यथा ..
सर्वं कथय तत्त्वेन सत्यसारा हि साधवः .. 3.3.8.130 ..
.. सूत उवाच ..
एतावदुक्त्वा नरदेवपुत्री सबाष्पकंठं सुचिरं रुरोद ..
मुमोह भूमौ पतिता सखीभिर्वृता न किंचित्कथितुं शशाक .. 31 ..
श्रुत्वा चंद्रांगदः सर्वं प्रियायाः शोककारणम् ..
मुहूर्त्तमभवतूष्णीं स्वयं शोकसमाकुलः .. 32 ..
अथाश्वास्य प्रियां तन्वीं विविधैर्वाक्यनैपुणैः ..

पुलकांचितसर्वांगीं तां कर्णे त्विदमब्रवीत् .. 34 ..
3.3.m:
"Who are you, resembling the god of love? Who are these two at your side?
Are you a god, a king, a siddha, a gandharva, or a kinnara?
Why do you inquire about my story as if full of affection?
Do you know me, O strong-armed one, or have you seen me somewhere?"
You appear to me as one seen before, like one of my own kin.
Tell everything in truth, for the good are founded on truth.”
Sūta said:
Having said this much, the king's daughter wept for a long time, her throat choked with tears.
Falling to the ground, surrounded by her female companions, she fainted and was unable to say anything.
Hearing all the cause of his beloved's grief, Candrāṅgada
remained silent for a moment, himself overwhelmed with sorrow.
Then, having consoled his slender-waisted beloved with various skillful words,
he said: “We are gods known as Siddhas, who can go wherever we wish.
Then, drawing close to her who feared being grasped by the hand, as if by force,
her entire body thrilled with horripilation, he whispered this in her ear:

3.3.s:
kvāpi loke mayā dṛṣṭastava bharttā varānane ..

3.3.d:
क्वापि लोके मया दृष्टस्तव भर्त्ता वरानने ..
त्वद्व्रताचरणात्प्रीतः सद्य एवागमिष्यति .. .. 35 ..
अपनेष्यति ते शोकं द्वित्रैरेव दिनैर्ध्रुवम् ..
एतच्छंसितुमायातस्तव भर्त्तुः सखाऽस्म्यहम् .. 36 ..
अत्र कार्यो न संदेहः शपामि शिवपादयोः ..
तावत्त्वद्धृदये स्थेयं न प्रकाश्यं च कुत्रचित् .. 37 ..

संभ्रमोद्भ्रांतनयना तमेव मुहुरैक्षत .. .. 38 ..
प्रेमबंधानुगुणितं वाक्यं चाह रसायनम् ..
विभ्रमोदारसहितं मधुरापांगवीक्षणम् .. 39 ..
स्वपाणिस्पर्शनोद्भिन्नपुलकांचितविग्रहम्..
पूर्व दृष्टानि चांगेषु लक्षणानि स्वरादिषु ..
वयःप्रमाणं वर्णं च परीक्ष्यैनमतर्कयत् .. 3.3.8.140 ..
एष एव पतिर्मे स्याद्ध्रुवं नान्यो भविष्यति ..
अस्मिन्नेव प्रसक्तं मे हृदयं प्रेमकातरम् .. 141 ..
3.3.m:
“In some world, O fair-faced lady, your husband was seen by me;
pleased by your observance of the vow, he will return right soon.
He will surely remove your grief in just two or three days.
I have come to announce this; I am your husband's friend.
No doubt should be harbored in this matter; I swear by the feet of Śiva.
Until then, it must remain in your heart and not be revealed anywhere.”
Hearing his speech, which surpassed a hundred streams of nectar,
she gazed at him again and again, her eyes bewildered with agitation.
He spoke words that were an elixir, multiplying the bonds of love,
accompanied by noble charm and casting sweet side-glances,
his body thrilled with horripilation bursting forth at the touch of his own hand [on hers].
Noticing the marks seen before on his limbs, his voice, and other [traits],
and examining his age, stature, and complexion, she pondered:
“This must indeed be my husband; surely he can be no other.
My heart, anxious with love, is attached to this very man.

3.3.s:
paralokādihāyātaḥ kathamevaṃ svarūpadhṛk ..

परलोकादिहायातः कथमेवं स्वरूपधृक् ..
दुर्भाग्यायाः कथं मे स्याद्भर्तुर्नष्टस्य दर्शनम् .. 142 ..
स्वप्नोयं किमु न स्वप्नो भ्रमोऽयं किं तु न भ्रमः ..
एष धूर्तोऽथवा कश्चिद्यक्षो गंधर्व एव वा .. 143 ..
मुनिपल्या यदुक्तं मे परमापद्गतापि च ..
व्रतमेतत्कुरुष्वेति तस्य वा फलमेव वा..44..
यो वर्षायुत सौभाग्यं ममेत्याह द्विजोत्तमः..

लज्जानम्रमुखीं कर्णे शशंसात्मप्रयोजनम् .. 47 ..

गच्छामः स्वस्ति ते भद्रे सद्यः पतिमवाप्स्यसि .. 48 ..
इत्युक्त्वाश्वं समारुह्य जगाम नृपनंदनः ..
3.3.m:
How could one have come here from the other world bearing such a form of his own?
How could there be a darśana of my lost husband for an unfortunate woman like me?
Is this a dream? But it is not a dream. Is this a delusion? Yet it is no delusion.
Is this a rogue, or some yakṣa or gandharva?
Or is this the fruit of that vow which the sage's wife told me [to perform],
saying, ‘Even if fallen into extreme distress, perform this vow’?
The excellent twice-born who said to me, ‘Your good fortune will last ten thousand years’—
surely his word was true; who could know except Īśvara?
Auspicious omens are also seen day after day.
When the Lord of Pārvatī is pleased, what is impossible for embodied beings?”
Reflecting thus in many ways, her doubts were dispelled; to her,
whose face was bowed with bashfulness, he declared his purpose in her ear:
“We are going to recount this event to his parents, who are tormented by grief.
Blessing to you, auspicious lady; you will regain your husband immediately.”
Having spoken thus and mounted his horse, the prince departed;

3.3.m:
together with those two, he reached his own kingdom in an instant.
Stationed near the city’s pleasure-grove, he dispatched that young serpent
to his kinsmen who were seated on the royal throne.
He went and said to them quickly: “Let Indrasena be released!
His son Candrāṅgada has arrived from the abode of the serpents.
Vacate the royal throne; do not hesitate!
Otherwise, the arrows of Candrāṅgada will swiftly take your lives!
He who sank into the waters of the Yamunā went to the mansion of Takṣaka,
and having obtained his assistance, has returned here from that world.”
Hearing that entire account related in full,
the adversaries, confounded, cried out, “Excellent, excellent!”
Then, having quickly reported to Indrasena the return of his lost son,
and having appeased him as he regained the royal throne, the chiefs among the kinsmen were seized with fear.
Then all the citizens, having seen the prince in the city park,

hastily reported it to the king and received great wealth.
Hearing that his son had arrived, the king was flooded with tears of joy;
neither he nor the queen, in their supreme delight, were aware of this world.
Then all the citizens, senior ministers, and domestic priests,
going out to meet him and embracing him, brought him before the king.
Then, having entered his own palace with a grand celebration,
the prince bowed to his parents, shedding tears. // 59
For a moment, the ruler of the earth did not recognize his own son who had fallen at his feet;
awakened by the ministers, he somehow stood up and embraced him with a moistened heart. // 3.3.8.160
In turn saluting his mothers, whose blessings were increased as they were overwhelmed with affection,
the king's son, embraced [by them], honored all the citizens. // 61
Seated in their midst, his entire story
he reported to his father, as well as the friendship of Takṣaka, // 62
and the heap of wealth consisting of jewels and the like given by the serpent king;

all that divine [wealth] brought by the Rākṣasas he offered to his father. // 63
Agitated upon seeing and hearing the deeds of the prince, / he considered it to be the good fortune of his daughter-in-law, earned by worshiping the Great Lord. // 64
This news full of auspiciousness the king of Niṣadha
reported through spies to King Citravarmā. // 65
Hearing the nectar-like report, he rose up in haste,
gave abundant wealth to them, and danced, overwhelmed with joy. // 66
Then, calling his daughter and embracing her with tearful eyes,
he adorned with ornaments her who had cast aside the marks of widowhood. // 67
Then there was a great festival in the realms, villages, cities, and the like;
people on all sides praised the auspicious conduct of Sīmantinī. // 68

offered his daughter to him again according to the rites of marriage. // 69
Candrāṅgada also, with jewels and other treasures brought from the abode of Takṣaka,
which were extremely difficult for mortals to obtain, adorned his own wife. // 3.3.8.170

With divine unguents gleaming like heated gold,
she shone with a fragrance spreading for ten yojanas. // 71
With an unfading garland of the perpetual color of lotus filaments,
produced from the wishing tree, the young, virtuous woman shone, beautifully adorned. // 72
Thus, having regained his wife at an auspicious time,
Candrāṅgada went back to his own city with the approval of his father-in-law. // 73
King Indrasena, having installed his own son upon the throne,
worshiped Śiva through austerity and attained the destination of self-restrained ascetics. // 74
For ten thousand years, together with his wife Sīmantinī,
King Candrāṅgada enjoyed many worldly pleasures. // 75
She gave birth to eight sons and one fair-faced daughter;
Sīmantinī took delight with her husband while worshiping the Great Lord,
and day by day obtained good fortune arising from the Monday [observance]. // 76
Sūta said:
This wondrous narrative has been thoroughly described by me;
I shall also declare again the māhātmya proclaimed regarding the Monday observance. // 177

3.3.m:
Sūta said:
Those who know the reality of Śiva—which consists of eternal bliss, is peaceful, free of conceptual differentiation, flawless, and without beginning or end—have attained the supreme state. / 1
Those steadfast ones who, detached from the pleasures of desires, practice unmotivated,
supreme devotion to Śiva attain liberation, not transmigration. / 2
Those who, while intending sensory objects, maintain affection for Śiva
are not overcome by sensory objects, even while enjoying their fruits. / 3
Endowed with devotion to Śiva with whatever disposition,
a man is not destroyed by time; he attains the supreme state. / 4
He who wishes to ascend to the supreme realm, but whose mind is attached to sensory objects,
should worship Śambhu through ritual action; at the end of enjoyment he shall attain Śiva. / 5
Almost no one is capable of abandoning the latent desire for sensory objects;
therefore, action-based worship is a wish-fulfilling cow for embodied souls. / 6
For those who, having enjoyed happiness for a long time even in this world composed of illusion,
desire liberation at the end of the body, this duty has been proclaimed. / 7
Worship of Śiva in this world is always the cause of heaven and final liberation,
especially on Monday when combined with auspicious qualities such as pradoṣa. / 8
For those who perform the worship of Śiva even merely on a Monday,
nothing whatsoever is difficult to obtain in this world or the next. / 9
Having fasted, become pure, and controlled one's senses on a Monday,
one should worship Śiva according to the rules, through Vedic or worldly rites. / 10
A celibate student, a householder, an unmarried girl, a married woman,
or a widow, having worshiped him, obtains the desired boon. / 11
Here I shall relate a story captivating to the listener's heart;
having heard it, they indeed attain liberation, and devotion directed to Śambhu arises. / 12
In Āryāvarta there was a certain king, the best of the upholders of righteousness,
renowned as Citravarman, a King of Justice to the wicked. / 13
He was the protector of the embankments of righteousness, the chastiser of those who walk on evil paths,
the performer of all sacrifices, the savior of those seeking refuge, / 14
the maker of all merits, the bestower of all riches,
the conqueror of hordes of rivals, devoted to Śiva and Mukunda. / 15

Having obtained mighty sons from his compliant wives, / he at last obtained one fair-faced daughter, long prayed for. / 16
Having obtained that daughter, as Himavat obtained Pārvatī by good fortune, / he considered himself like a god, his desires fulfilled. / 17
Once, summoning virtuous leaders of the twice-born who knew the signs of horoscopes, / his mind filled with curiosity, he asked the consequences of the girl's birth. / 18
Then one excellent twice-born [brahmin] there, learned in many matters, said: / “This daughter of yours, O king, shall be named Sīmantinī. / 19
She will be auspicious like Umā, beautiful like Damayantī, / skilled in arts like Bhāratī, endowed with great virtues like Lakṣmī. / 20
She will have good offspring like the Mother of the Gods, be devoted to vows like Jānakī, / radiant with noble splendor like the light of the sun, delightful like the moonlight. / 21
For ten thousand years she will rejoice with her husband; / having borne eight sons, she will attain supreme happiness.” / 22
When he had spoken thus, the king, honoring that twice-born [brahmin] with wealth, / experienced supreme joy, drinking the nectar of his words. / 23
Then another twice-born [brahmin] too, steadfast and of immeasurable splendor, spoke: / “In her fourteenth year, she will meet with widowhood.” / 24
Hearing his word, harsh as a thunderbolt's crash, / the king for a moment became bewildered in his mind with sorrow. / 25
Then, dismissing all the brahmins, the king, lover of the sacred word, / considered everything to be ordained by fate and became free of anxiety. / 26
And that young girl Sīmantinī, her childhood gradually passing, / heard from the mouth of her own friend of her future widowhood. / 27
Having fallen into deep despair, the maiden pondered; / she approached Maitreyī, the wife of the sage Yājñavalkya, and questioned her: / 28
“O mother, distressed with fear, I have sought refuge at your lotus feet; / you ought to declare to me an action that promotes good fortune in marriage.” / 29
To the king's daughter who had thus sought refuge, the virtuous wife of the sage said:

“Take refuge, O slender-limbed girl, in Pārvatī united with Śiva. / 30
On Mondays worship Śiva and Gaurī with a collected mind, / having fasted or bathed well, wearing spotless garments. / 31
Restraining speech with an unwavering mind, having performed the proper worship, / and having fed brahmins, properly propitiate Śiva. / 32
Destruction of sins comes through anointing; imperial rule from worshiping the pedestal; / all good fortune and happiness from offering perfumes, garlands, and unhusked grain. / 33
Sweet fragrance comes from presenting incense, and radiant splendor from presenting a lamp; / great enjoyment from food offerings, and prosperity from offering betel. / 34
Virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation come from offering salutations; / recitation of mantras is indeed the cause of the perfections such as the eight sovereign powers. / 35
From oblation in fire arises the fulfillment of all desires; / from feeding brahmins comes the satisfaction of all the gods. / 36
In this manner worship Śiva and also Śivā on Mondays; / even if overtaken by terrible misfortune, you will overcome defeat. / 37
Even if fallen into most terrible, awful, and frightening misery, / by the power of worshiping Śiva you will cross over great fear.” / 38
Having thus properly instructed Sīmantinī, the virtuous woman departed; / and that princess of lovely hips did accordingly. / 39
To Damayantī and Nala was born a son named Indrasena; / his son was Candrāṅgada, resembling the moon. / 40
Citravarmā, best of kings, summoning that prince, / gave his daughter Sīmantinī to him with the permission of his preceptors. / 41
There was a great festival at her wedding, / where a great gathering of all kings took place. / 42
Having taken her hand in marriage at the appointed time, the fortunate Candrāṅgada / lived for some months right there in his father-in-law's house. / 43
Once, to cross the Yamunā, that powerful prince / boarded a boat playfully with some companions. / 44

the boat, struck by a whirlpool, sank along with the boatmen. / 45
A very great cry of “Alas, alas!” arose on both its banks; / as all the troops looked on, their wailing touched the sky. / 46
Drowning, some died; some went into the bellies of crocodiles; / the prince and others were not seen anywhere in the vast water. / 47
Hearing that, King Citravarmā too, utterly distracted, / reached the bank of the Yamunā and became motionless. / 48
Hearing it, the king's wives too lost consciousness; / and Sīmantinī, upon hearing it, fell unconscious to the ground. / 49
Likewise the other chief ministers, generals, and family priests, / bewildered and tormented by grief, wailed with their hair disheveled. / 50
King Indrasena also, deeply afflicted upon hearing the news of his son, / fell down senseless together with his wives. / 51
His ministers, his citizens, and the inhabitants of that land, / including children, the elderly, and women, cried out, overcome with grief. / 52
Out of grief, some beat their chests and some beat their heads; / they wandered about crying, “Alas, prince! Alas, dear one! Where are you? Where are you?” / 53
Thus the city of King Indrasena, full of sorrow and miserable, / was suddenly agitated, and likewise the city of Citravarmā. / 54
Then King Citravarmā, consoled by the elders, / slowly went to the city and comforted his daughter. / 55
Together with the relatives who had arrived, the king had the funeral rites / performed completely for that son-in-law who had drowned in the water. / 56
And that virtuous woman Sīmantinī, intent on [reaching] the world of her husband, / though dissuaded by her father out of affection, assumed widowhood. / 57
That auspicious Monday vow which had been taught by the sage's wife, / she of auspicious conduct did not abandon, even though she had met with widowhood. / 58
Having thus met with severe suffering in her fourteenth year, / meditating on the lotus feet of Śiva, she spent three years. / 59

3.3.m: Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled 'Description of the Instruction of Ṛṣabha to Bhadrāyu', in the Brahmakhaṇḍa, the third [part] of the eighty-one-thousand-verse collection of the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa.
Ṛṣabha said:
Bowing to Mahādeva, the all-pervading Īśvara,
I shall declare the armour consisting of Śiva, which affords all protection to men.
Seated in a clean place, with a seat prepared according to rule,
with senses subdued and breath controlled, one should contemplate the imperishable Śiva.
Seated within the lotus of the heart, pervading the space of the sky with his own splendour,
beyond the senses, subtle, endless, primeval, full of supreme bliss—one should meditate on Maheśa.
With the bond of all action shaken off through meditation, mind long immersed in the bliss of consciousness,
with oneself concentrated through the placement of the six syllables, one should make protection with the Śaiva armour:

3.3.m: Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, to Sadāśiva, whose self is all principles of reality, whose sport is all principles of reality, the sole creator of all worlds, the sole sustainer of all worlds, the sole destroyer of all worlds, the sole teacher of all worlds, the sole witness of all worlds, secret to all scriptures, giver of all boons, crusher of all afflictions caused by sins, granter of fearlessness to all the world, the sole bringer of welfare to all worlds, who bears the crescent moon upon his crest, whose radiance is eternal and inherent, devoid of qualities, beyond comparison, formless, without semblance, free from disease, devoid of cosmic manifoldness, stainless, beyond duality, unattached, pure, free from departure, possessing eternal power of form, of incomparable power, without support, eternal, pure, awakened, complete, existence-consciousness-bliss, non-dual, having the nature of supreme peaceful luminous light! / Hail, hail, O Mahārudra, of great fierceness, auspicious manifestation, tearer of the forest fire of grief, Mahābhairava, Kālabhairava, Bhairava of the aeon’s end, wearer of a garland of skulls, terrifying with a thousand hands holding weapons: the skull-topped staff, sword, shield, noose, goad, drum, trident, bow, arrows, mace, spear, bhindipāla, javelin, pestle, mallet, paṭṭiśa, axe, iron club, bhuśuṇḍi, śataghnī, discus, and others; dreadful with bared fangs in your mouth; who expands the sphere of the universe with violent loud laughter; wearing earrings of lordly serpents, a necklace of lordly serpents, bracelets of lordly serpents, clad in the hide of the king of serpents; conqueror of death, Tryambaka, destroyer of Tripura, Virūpākṣa, lord of the universe, universal form, whose mount is the bull, adorned with poison, facing every direction! Guard, guard me on all sides! Blaze, blaze! Destroy, destroy the fear of great death and untimely death! Uproot, uproot the fear of disease! Quell, quell the fear of venomous serpents! Kill, kill the fear of thieves! Drive away, drive away my enemies! Pierce, pierce with the trident! Break, break with the battle-axe! Cut, cut with the sword! Crush, crush with the skull-topped staff! Grind to powder, grind to powder with the pestle! Strike, strike with your arrows! Terrify, terrify the rākṣasas! Put the bhūtas to flight, put them to flight! Cause utter panic to kūṣmāṇḍas, vetālas, the host of Mārīs, and brahma-rākṣasas! Grant, grant me fearlessness! Reassure, reassure me who am terrified! Deliver, deliver me from the fear of hell! Revive, revive me! Nourish, nourish me who am afflicted by hunger and thirst! Delight, delight me who am tormented by sorrow! Clothe, clothe me with the armour of Śiva! O Tryambaka, O Sadāśiva, homage to you, homage to you, homage to you!

There is a certain Śivayogin named Vāmadeva, of great austerity.
